title: Q3 carrier rates fall 3.3% per package; operators capture 0.6%
sum: Carrier rates fell 3.3% per package in the third quarter, but operators captured 0.6% in actual savings, according to Commerce Signal data discussed by Deposco's Eric Lemus. He attributed the gap to heavier packages, faster service levels and more residential deliveries.
plain: No rate or service change takes effect. The analysis says Q3 per-package carrier rates fell 3.3%, but heavier, faster and more residential shipments left operators with 0.6% in savings.
why: An industry analysis says shipment mix shifts offset a 3.3% per-package rate decline, leaving operators with 0.6% in savings in Q3.
syn: Carrier rates fell 3.3% per package in the third quarter, but operators captured just 0.6% in actual savings, according to Commerce Signal data discussed by Eric Lemus, vice president of strategy and analytics at Deposco. Lemus said the gap came from a shift toward heavier packages, faster service levels and more residential deliveries, not from contract negotiations. He said sub-5-pound package costs declined, but volume surged in the 11-to-20-pound tier. Lemus also said brands entered peak with about 94 days of inventory against 91 days for third-party logistics providers, which he said makes stockouts a central risk for Cyber Week and Q4.

aff.what: Per-package carrier rates fell 3.3%, but operators captured just 0.6% in actual savings, per the analysis.
Volume surged in this tier, offsetting lower costs on sub-5-pound packages, Lemus said.
Brands held 94 days of inventory versus 91 for 3PLs; Lemus said stockouts could mean higher expedited-service costs.
Deposco is tracking rising peak shipping costs relative to Q3 and near-daily fuel-surcharge shifts, Lemus said.

title: Amazon readers split over $5 fee warning on NYC bill
sum: Business Insider said its readers are divided over Amazon's app and website notice opposing the Delivery Protection Act. The notice says Amazon would raise fees by up to $5 per order if the bill becomes law. The bill is before the New York City Council and would require companies like Amazon to directly employ delivery drivers rather than use contractors.
plain: No fee or service change has taken effect. Amazon says it would raise fees by up to $5 per order if the Delivery Protection Act becomes law.
why: The bill would require companies like Amazon to directly employ NYC delivery drivers, and Amazon says it would add up to $5 per order if it passes.
new: Business Insider reported on reader reactions to Amazon's in-app notice, with commenters split between support for worker protections and concern for contracted delivery businesses; no change to the bill's status was reported.
syn: Business Insider reported that readers are split over Amazon's notice, in its app and on its website, opposing the Delivery Protection Act. The bill, before the New York City Council with Mayor Zohran Mamdani's support, would require companies like Amazon to directly employ delivery drivers instead of using contractors. Amazon's notice says it would raise fees by up to $5 per order if the measure becomes law. Some commenters backed the bill as a benefit to delivery workers. Others said it could hurt businesses that contract with Amazon as delivery service providers.

aff.who: Amazon customers in New York City
aff.what: Amazon says fees would rise by up to $5 per order if the Delivery Protection Act becomes law.
Some commenters said the bill could hurt the contractor businesses Amazon uses for delivery.
The bill would require companies like Amazon to employ drivers directly rather than use contractors.

title: Advent, FedEx, A&R and PPF complete InPost acquisition
sum: A consortium of Advent International, FedEx, A&R and PPF completed its acquisition of InPost, which is now fully privately owned. The consortium exercised squeeze-out rights over the remaining shares on November 17, after reaching 98.49% ownership. InPost will stay operationally independent under its brand, with headquarters in Poland.
plain: No change to rates or service has been announced. InPost and FedEx have entered commercial agreements that let selected recipients use InPost's last-mile network in Europe.
why: InPost runs over 100,000 out-of-home locations, and FedEx is now a 37% co-owner of the consortium that controls the network.
tie: Settlement of the public takeover offer took place on September 30, followed by the consortium's rise to 98.49% ownership and its November 17 exercise of squeeze-out rights, according to grafa.com.
syn: InPost S.A. was acquired by a consortium of Advent International, FedEx, A&R and PPF, which completed the deal after settlement of the public takeover offer on September 30. The consortium reached 98.49% ownership after the post-acceptance period and exercised squeeze-out rights over the remaining shares on November 17. InPost will remain operationally independent with its headquarters in Poland and Rafał Brzoska as CEO. The consortium plans to speed up investment in InPost's European out-of-home network, and InPost and FedEx have entered commercial agreements giving selected recipients access to InPost's last-mile network.

aff.what: Advent International and FedEx each hold 37% of the consortium, A&R holds 16% and PPF holds 10%.
Selected recipients can use InPost's last-mile capabilities and out-of-home infrastructure under commercial agreements.
The consortium plans more investment in the technology and network, which spans over 100,000 locations.

title: FedEx names Jamere Jackson CFO, effective Nov. 30
sum: FedEx Corp. appointed Jamere Jackson chief financial officer, effective Nov. 30, according to the company announcement. He succeeds Claude Russ, who has been interim CFO since June 1. Jackson was most recently CFO of AutoZone.
plain: No change to rates or service. The appointment affects FedEx's finance leadership only.
why: The appointment fills the finance chief role at FedEx, which has had an interim CFO since June 1.
syn: FedEx Corp. has appointed Jamere Jackson chief financial officer, effective Nov. 30. He succeeds Claude Russ, who has served as interim CFO since June 1. Jackson was most recently CFO of AutoZone, where he also led Store Development, and earlier held CFO roles at Hertz Global Holdings and Nielsen Holdings. FedEx CEO Raj Subramaniam said Jackson's leadership will support the company's drive for profitable growth.

aff.what: No change to rates or service.
Jackson becomes CFO on Nov. 30, replacing interim CFO Claude Russ.

title: Waymo, Serve Robotics move away from exclusive Uber deals, The Verge reports
sum: The Verge reported that Waymo plans to end its exclusive robotaxi partnership with Uber in Austin and Atlanta, with riders able to hail rides in the Waymo app from January 2028. Serve Robotics said it will not renew its Uber Eats partnership when it expires in 2027 and has launched a direct developer API.
plain: No change to parcel rates or service. Waymo riders in Austin and Atlanta can use the Waymo app directly from January 2028, and Serve's Uber Eats partnership expires in 2027.
why: Serve runs more than 2,000 sidewalk robots; its exit from Uber Eats in 2027 points robot delivery toward direct business access instead of delivery apps.
tie: The report says Uber's CEO described the Waymo partnership as very strong on an August earnings call, weeks before Waymo's co-CEO said it would end the exclusive deal.
syn: The Verge reported that Waymo and Serve Robotics are walking away from exclusive arrangements with Uber. Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana said the company would end its exclusive robotaxi partnership in Austin and Atlanta, calling the mixed-fleet experience a "crapshoot"; riders can hail driverless rides in the Waymo app from January 2028. Serve, which operates more than 2,000 sidewalk robots, will not renew its Uber Eats deal when it expires in 2027 and launched a direct developer API. Uber said it raised concerns about Serve's operational performance and reliability beginning in early 2026.

aff.who: Waymo riders in Austin and Atlanta
aff.what: Can hail driverless rides directly in the Waymo app starting January 2028.
Serve Robotics will not renew its partnership when it expires in 2027.
Serve's developer API lets any small business build robot delivery on Serve's fleet, without delivery-app fees of 15 to 30 percent.

title: Zipline plans Phoenix drone delivery launch for early 2027, FAA documents show
sum: Zipline is preparing to expand drone delivery into the Phoenix area and hopes to serve Valley customers in early 2027, according to a 12News report published via Yahoo. An FAA draft environmental assessment outlines up to 65,000 deliveries a day each in Phoenix and Tucson, and the FAA is taking public comments through Dec. 7, 2026.
plain: No change to rates or service now. Zipline hopes to start serving Phoenix-area customers in early 2027, pending additional FAA authorization.
why: The FAA draft assessment allows up to 130,000 daily drone deliveries across Phoenix and Tucson, a potential scale for local last-mile drone service.
new: Zipline's planned Arizona expansion and the FAA draft assessment's capacity figures of up to 130,000 daily deliveries add a new market to the Texas launches, with no change to shipper rates or service yet.
syn: Zipline is preparing to expand drone delivery into the Phoenix metropolitan area and hopes to begin serving customers there in early 2027. An FAA draft environmental assessment describes potential operations of up to 65,000 deliveries per day in Phoenix and another 65,000 in Tucson, or 130,000 combined, involving up to 390,000 flight segments. Zipline's community engagement lead Zach Hill said the figures represent potential capacity, not expected volume at launch. The FAA is accepting public comments through Dec. 7, 2026.

aff.what: Zipline hopes to begin drone deliveries in the Valley in early 2027; participating businesses and neighborhoods are not yet announced.
Up to 130 charging facilities and 2,600 package pickup kiosks across Phoenix and Tucson, per the FAA draft assessment.
Zipline is seeking additional FAA authorization for Arizona; public comments on the draft assessment are open through Dec. 7, 2026.

title: NYC lawmakers weigh replacing Amazon direct-hire mandate with options
sum: New York City lawmakers are considering replacing the Delivery Protection Act's direct-hire mandate with a menu of options, Transport Topics reported, citing people with knowledge of the matter. Amazon could employ workers directly, use carriers such as UPS or the U.S. Postal Service, or contract with fully independent third-party operators. If lawmakers reach an agreement, a vote could come within a few weeks.
plain: No rate or service change has taken effect. The bill is still under negotiation, and a City Council vote could come within a few weeks if lawmakers reach an agreement, according to the people cited.
why: About 40 Amazon delivery service partners operate in the city, and the changes would alter how Amazon runs its last-mile network there.
new: Lawmakers are weighing replacing the direct-hire mandate with a menu of options, which would let Amazon keep its delivery partners if they gain independence, and a vote could follow within a few weeks.
syn: New York City lawmakers are discussing a compromise on the Delivery Protection Act that would drop the requirement that Amazon directly hire delivery workers, according to people with knowledge of the matter cited by Transport Topics. Amazon would instead choose between direct employment, carriers such as UPS or the U.S. Postal Service, or fully independent third-party operators, which would control their own routes, quotas and hiring. Amazon and local delivery companies had opposed the original bill; about 40 Amazon delivery service partners operate in the city. A Council vote could come within a few weeks if an agreement is reached.

aff.what: Would choose among direct hiring, carriers like UPS or USPS, or independent operators, and face greater city oversight.
About 40 firms in the city would gain autonomy over routes, quotas, hiring and discipline under the options discussed.
Amazon and others would still need a city license from the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection.

title: Reason column defends Amazon DSP model against NJ antitrust suit
sum: An opinion piece in Reason Magazine argues that New Jersey's August monopsony suit against Amazon's delivery service partner (DSP) network is misguided. The piece also covers a New York City bill that would require Amazon to hire its contractors' drivers directly. Amazon began warning New York shoppers this week that the bill could add as much as $5 to each order, according to the piece.
plain: No rates or service change now. The piece says the NJ suit could lead to "structural relief" for Amazon's contractor network, and the NYC bill could add as much as $5 per order, according to Amazon.
why: The NJ suit and the NYC bill both target Amazon's contractor-based last-mile model, which the piece says delivered more parcels than FedEx or UPS last year.

title: Walmart says sub-30-minute delivery volume surged in Q3
sum: Walmart's U.S. sub-30-minute delivery volume surged in the third quarter, according to Supply Chain Dive's report on the retailer's earnings call. U.S. President and CEO David Guggina said faster pick times at stores could speed deliveries further. Executives said U.S. online sales jumped as customers chose fast delivery options.
plain: No change to rates or service is announced. Walmart said demand for its fastest delivery options grew in Q3 and that faster in-store picking could shorten delivery times.
why: Walmart is one of the largest U.S. retailers, and its growth in fast local delivery shows where consumer demand for speed is heading.
syn: Walmart said volume of its sub-30-minute deliveries surged in the third quarter, according to Supply Chain Dive, which reported on the retailer's earnings call. Executives said U.S. online sales jumped as customers chose fast delivery options. U.S. President and CEO David Guggina said faster pick times at stores could speed up deliveries even further. The source text available did not include volume figures.

aff.what: Executives said customers increasingly used fast delivery options in Q3, and faster store pick times could shorten delivery times.
No change to rates or service.

title: Amazon's Larsen details ASCS, rural delivery build-out on podcast
sum: Logistics Management published a podcast with Peter Larsen, the Amazon vice president who leads Amazon Supply Chain Services (ASCS). According to the episode description, topics include the May 2026 ASCS rollout, a $4 billion investment to triple Amazon's delivery network by the end of 2026, expanded less-than-truckload offerings and a fleet of more than 50,000 electric delivery vans.
plain: No change to rates or service is announced. The episode description lists the ASCS rollout, the delivery network investment and LTL offerings as topics.
why: The episode description says Amazon is putting $4 billion into tripling its delivery network, with a focus on small towns and rural areas.
syn: Logistics Management published a podcast episode featuring Peter Larsen, a Vice President at Amazon who leads Amazon Supply Chain Services (ASCS). ASCS offers businesses access to Amazon's freight, distribution, fulfillment and parcel shipping capabilities. The episode description lists the May 2026 ASCS rollout and a $4 billion investment toward tripling Amazon's delivery network by the end of 2026, focused on small towns and rural areas. It also lists expanded LTL offerings available through ASCS and progress on a fleet of more than 50,000 electric delivery vans.

aff.what: $4 billion investment toward tripling the network by end of 2026, focused on small towns and rural areas.
ASCS launched in May 2026, with expanded LTL offerings now available through the service.
The episode cites progress with a fleet of more than 50,000 electric delivery vans.

title: NYC delivery bill opponents add legal, racial arguments against Intro 518
sum: Opponents of the New York City Delivery Protection Act (Intro 518), led by the New York Delivers Coalition, have held rallies and sent a nine-page letter to Council Speaker Julie Menin arguing the bill conflicts with federal and state law, FreightWaves reported. A vote is possible before the end of the year on an amended version. The New York Post cited Amazon's warning that the bill could add $5 to every package it delivers in the city.
plain: No rates or service have changed. If the bill passes as originally worded, Amazon would have to buy about 100 city delivery service providers, and Amazon says it could add $5 per package.
why: The bill could force Amazon to bring about 100 city delivery service providers in-house, and FedEx would also be affected, according to FreightWaves.
tie: Amazon told New York City customers on Nov. 19, 2026 that Intro 518 could add up to $5 per order, and an Amazon-led business coalition threatened suit in a letter to Menin in November 2026, according to earlier coverage.
new: Opponents added a nine-page legal letter to Speaker Menin, citing federal preemption under F4A, state law conflicts and a consulting firm's estimate of 3,000 to more than 10,000 job losses; no rates or service have changed for shippers yet.

title: UPS Healthcare, Medvantx open expanded pharmacy near Worldport
sum: UPS Healthcare and Medvantx opened an expanded, fully licensed pharmacy near UPS Worldport in Louisville, UPS said in a story dated Nov. 19, 2026. UPS said the site adds cold storage and later shipping windows for direct-to-patient deliveries. The companies have worked together for 10 years.
plain: No change to UPS rates or fees. The expanded pharmacy offers later pick, pack and ship times for prescriptions moving through Worldport, according to UPS.
why: The site gives pharmacy shippers later pick-up times and cold storage next to UPS's largest air hub, per UPS; no rates or fees are involved.
syn: UPS Healthcare and Medvantx opened an expanded, fully licensed pharmacy near UPS Worldport, UPS said in a story dated Nov. 19, 2026. UPS described Worldport as its largest global air hub. The company said the space adds cold storage, later shipping windows and room to grow for direct-to-patient deliveries. The companies have worked together for 10 years, according to UPS. Medvantx CEO Kurt Browning said the later pick, pack and ship times are a critical advantage.

aff.what: Expanded licensed pharmacy near Worldport with more cold storage, per UPS.
Later pick, pack and ship times with quick access to Worldport, per UPS.

title: Amazon faces NYC bill that would end subcontracting for 5,000 delivery workers
sum: Amazon employs more than 40 local delivery companies with over 5,000 workers in New York City, and a proposed Delivery Protection Act would require large last-mile operators to hold city licenses and hire drivers directly, TradingView reported. Amazon said the bill could force it to consider moving delivery facilities outside the city and estimated it could add up to $5 to each order. Negotiations with the company and labor representatives continue.
plain: No change has taken effect. If the bill becomes law, Amazon says order costs in New York City could rise by up to $5 and its local delivery operations could move outside the city.
why: The bill would affect Amazon's 15 New York City last-mile facilities and more than 5,000 delivery workers, with Amazon estimating up to $5 more per order.
tie: Amazon told New York City customers on 2026-11-19 that Intro 518 could add up to $5 per order, and in a Nov. 16 letter a coalition led by Amazon said it could sue if the bill passes in its current form.
new: TradingView adds that Amazon employs more than 40 local delivery companies with over 5,000 workers and that talks continue, with the bill's financial impact unknown until it is enacted.
syn: New York City lawmakers are weighing the Delivery Protection Act, which would require last-mile facility operators to obtain city licenses and turn some subcontracting relationships into direct employment, TradingView reported. Amazon said it employs more than 40 local delivery companies with over 5,000 workers in the city and that the bill could endanger those partnerships and lead it to consider moving facilities outside the city. Amazon estimated the requirements could add up to $5 to each customer order but has not publicly detailed the calculation. Supporters, including labor groups and Mayor Zohran Mamdani, said direct hiring would improve worker safety, accountability and labor protections. The financial impact is unknown until the bill is enacted, according to the article.

aff.what: More than 40 local delivery companies with over 5,000 workers could lose subcontracting arrangements, Amazon said.
Amazon estimates the requirements could add up to $5 to each order; the calculation is not public.
Published reports say Amazon runs 15 such facilities in the city; they would need city licenses.
Amazon says the changes could slow deliveries and make them more expensive.

title: Uber Eats adds AutoParts.com as first auto parts retailer
sum: Uber Technologies and AutoParts.com announced on Nov. 19 that AutoParts.com is the first auto parts retailer on Uber Eats. Customers across the U.S. can order from nearly 7,000 participating locations for on-demand or scheduled delivery, according to Traction News.
plain: No change to carrier rates or fees. Uber Eats customers in the U.S. can now order auto parts from AutoParts.com locations for on-demand or scheduled delivery.
why: Uber Eats extends its retail delivery marketplace to auto parts, with nearly 7,000 participating locations available for on-demand or scheduled delivery.
syn: Uber Technologies and AutoParts.com announced on Nov. 19 that AutoParts.com has joined Uber Eats as the first auto parts retailer on the platform. Customers across the U.S. can shop inventory from nearly 7,000 participating locations in AutoParts.com's marketplace and fulfillment network, and choose on-demand or scheduled delivery. Uber called the launch a continued expansion of its retail marketplace into everyday items.

aff.what: Can order auto parts from AutoParts.com for on-demand or scheduled delivery across the U.S.
Nearly 7,000 participating locations can be reached through the Uber Eats app.
20% off AutoParts.com orders of $60 or more, up to $20 off, for a limited time in the U.S.

title: Amazon warns NYC customers Intro 518 could add up to $5 per order
sum: Amazon sent a message to New York City customers saying Intro 518, under consideration by the City Council, could add up to $5 per order. Amazon said it would no longer be able to work with its network of small delivery businesses if the bill passes and would consider moving operations outside the city. The company asked customers to contact their Council members.
plain: Nothing has changed in rates or service yet. Amazon says that if Intro 518 passes, New York City customers could pay up to $5 more per order and face slower, more expensive delivery.
why: The bill could change how Amazon delivers to New York City, where Amazon says it uses a network of small delivery businesses and millions of customers could see slower, costlier delivery.
tie: Amazon, the National Urban League and a business coalition warned in a Nov. 2026 letter to Speaker Julie Menin that they could sue if the Council passes Intro 518 in its current form.
new: Amazon is now telling New York City customers directly that Intro 518 could add up to $5 per order and slow delivery, a cost claim not in earlier coverage; the bill has not passed and no rates have changed.

title: project44 survey: 54% of shoppers would pay more for on-time holiday delivery
sum: project44 released its annual State of Consumer Holiday Shopping Report on Nov. 19, 2026. It said 54% of the 2,470 consumers surveyed worldwide would pay higher prices to guarantee gifts arrive in time for the holidays. The company also said 39% of shoppers had not planned to start holiday shopping until mid-November or later.
plain: No change to rates or service. The survey reports shopper attitudes toward holiday delivery, not carrier pricing.
why: The survey of 2,470 consumers gives retailers and shippers a measure of how much shoppers value delivery-date certainty over speed during peak.
syn: project44 released its annual State of Consumer Holiday Shopping Report on Nov. 19, 2026. According to the company, 54% of the 2,470 consumers surveyed worldwide said they would pay higher prices to guarantee gifts arrive in time for the holidays. It said shoppers care more about when a package arrives than how fast it moves, and that 39% had not planned to begin holiday shopping until mid-November or later. The survey closed on Nov. 3, 2026, and was run through SurveyMonkey among adults aged 18 and older.

aff.what: 54% of 2,470 surveyed said they would pay higher prices to guarantee on-time holiday arrival.
project44 said shoppers link late delivery to lost repeat business.
39% had not planned to start holiday shopping until mid-November or later.

title: USPS OIG report finds criminal groups recruiting postal employees
sum: The USPS Office of Inspector General said in its Fall 2026 Semiannual Report to Congress that criminal organizations are increasingly recruiting postal employees for mail theft and narcotics schemes. One Detroit case involved more than 10,000 stolen checks valued at about $63 million.
plain: No change to rates or service. The report describes insider crime cases and security weaknesses at USPS.
why: The OIG report points to insider involvement in mail theft and drug cases inside the USPS network, which carries mail and packages for shippers.
syn: The USPS Office of Inspector General said in its Fall 2026 Semiannual Report to Congress that it is finding more cases of collusion between postal employees and larger criminal organizations, rather than isolated wrongdoing. According to the report, syndicates target postal workers for their knowledge of and access to the network, and recruit in person and on social media. The report cites a Detroit case in which two mail processing facility employees stole checks, with more than 10,000 checks worth about $63 million advertised for sale, and a Puerto Rico case in which a retail clerk diverted packages containing cocaine.

aff.what: OIG said criminal groups recruit them in person and on social media for mail theft and drug schemes.
OIG said they remain targets because of universal arrow keys, and lost or stolen keys are an ongoing problem.
Audits found weaknesses in how USPS tracks and reports missing arrow keys; OIG said high-security collection box management could improve.

title: Amazon runs in-app notices opposing NYC Delivery Protection Act
sum: Amazon began showing some New York City customers app and website notices on Thursday saying Intro 518, the Delivery Protection Act, "could add up to $5 per order," CNBC and Business Insider reported. The bill would require last-mile delivery providers to hire workers as employees and has the backing of Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Amazon said it would consider moving operations outside the city if the bill passes.
plain: No change to rates or service yet. Amazon says New York City customers could face up to $5 more per order if the City Council passes Intro 518, which is awaiting review by Speaker Julie Menin.
why: Intro 518 would end the contractor model Amazon has used since 2018 for last-mile delivery, and Amazon says it could add up to $5 per order in New York City.
new: Amazon moved its opposition into its shopping app and website, with notices telling some New York City customers the bill could add up to $5 per order and directing them to contact council members; the bill has not passed and no fee has been set.
syn: Amazon began showing some New York City customers pop-ups and a homepage banner on its app and website on Thursday, saying Intro 518 "could add up to $5 per order," according to CNBC and Business Insider. The Delivery Protection Act would require last-mile providers to employ delivery workers directly, ending the contractor model Amazon has used since 2018. Amazon said it would be unable to work with its delivery partners if the bill passes and would consider moving operations outside the city. The bill was introduced in February, is awaiting review by Council Speaker Julie Menin, and has the backing of Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Teamsters.

aff.who: Amazon customers in New York City
aff.what: Amazon says the bill could add up to $5 per order; no price change has taken effect.
Amazon said it could no longer work with them if the bill passes.

aff.who: New York City delivery speed and cost
aff.what: Amazon said moving operations out of the city would likely mean slower, more expensive delivery.

title: DHL Express EBIT rises 50% in Q3 as Post & Parcel Germany profit falls
sum: An industry analysis of DHL's Q3 2026 results says group revenue rose 12.6% year-on-year to €22.6bn and EBIT rose 16.2% to €1.7bn. DHL Express EBIT rose 50% to €1bn, while Post & Parcel Germany EBIT fell 29.8% to €153m.
plain: No change to rates or service. The item reports DHL's quarterly financial results.
why: DHL Express's Q3 EBIT of €1bn contrasts with lower profit at DHL eCommerce and Post & Parcel Germany, according to an industry analysis.
syn: An industry analysis of DHL's Q3 2026 results says group revenue rose 12.6% year-on-year to €22.6bn and EBIT rose 16.2% to €1.7bn. DHL Express revenue rose 19.2% to €6.99bn and EBIT rose 50% to €1bn, a 14.8% margin, which the analysis attributes to premium 'Time Definite International' services. Post & Parcel Germany EBIT fell 29.8% to €153m on revenue up 0.3% at €4.2bn, and DHL eCommerce EBIT fell 70% despite organic revenue growth of around 6%.

aff.what: Q3 revenue up 19.2% to €6.99bn; EBIT up 50% to €1bn; EBIT margin 14.8%.
EBIT down 29.8% to €153m on revenue up 0.3% to €4.2bn, with DHL citing wage and de minimis factors.
Organic revenue up around 6%; EBIT down 70%; EBIT margin 3.2%.

aff.who: DHL Global Forwarding and Supply Chain
aff.what: EBIT up 32.7% and 8.1% respectively year-on-year.

title: USPS final rule sets 5.9% increase for competitive products
sum: The Postal Service published a final rule amending the Domestic Mail Manual for competitive product prices and mailing standards, effective January 17, 2027. Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail and USPS Ground Advantage prices rise 5.9 percent overall, and Parcel Select Destination Entry rises an average of 5.9 percent.
plain: From January 17, 2027, USPS competitive product prices rise 5.9 percent overall for Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail and USPS Ground Advantage. Several extra and mailer service fees rise by 8.0 to 9.1 percent.
why: Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, USPS Ground Advantage and Parcel Select prices all rise on Jan. 17, 2027, with some service fees rising faster.
tie: The rule follows USPS's Nov. 12, 2026 filing with the Postal Regulatory Commission proposing a 5.9% average increase and a permanent 11% fuel surcharge for the same Jan. 17, 2027 date.

dates.w: USPS competitive prices rise 5.9% overall; service fees change

new: The Federal Register final rule confirms the 5.9% overall increase and the Jan. 17, 2027 effective date, and gives specific fees, including 8.0% to 9.1% rises for several mailer services, that the earlier filing coverage did not detail.
syn: The Postal Service published a final rule in the Federal Register amending the Domestic Mail Manual to reflect competitive product price and mailing standards changes effective January 17, 2027. Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail and USPS Ground Advantage prices rise 5.9 percent overall, Parcel Select Destination Entry rises an average of 5.9 percent, and USPS Connect Local rises 6.0 percent. Extra service and other fees also rise, and the Dimension Noncompliance Fee is renamed and revised in its second phase. The new prices are available under Docket Number CP2027-1 on the Postal Regulatory Commission website.

aff.who: Priority Mail Express and Priority Mail shippers
aff.what: Prices rise 5.9 percent overall from January 17, 2027; the Express Flat Rate Envelope goes to $34.90.
Retail and Commercial prices each rise 5.9 percent from January 17, 2027.
Destination Entry rises an average of 5.9 percent; USPS Connect Local rises 6.0 percent.

aff.who: Users of extra and other services
aff.what: Adult Signature up 8.2 and 8.0 percent, Package Intercept up 8.0 percent, Nonstandard Fees up an average of 16 percent.

title: IDS first-half revenue rises 6.3% to £6.85bn as parcel volumes gain 8%
sum: IDS, the parent of Royal Mail and GLS, reported group revenue up 6.3% year on year to £6.85 billion in the first half, with parcel volumes up 8% to 1.2 billion. Royal Mail revenue rose 3.9% to £4.13 billion and GLS revenue rose 10.2% to £2.73 billion. IDS also said Royal Mail CEO Alistair Cochrane will retire at the end of 2026, with Paul Ablin taking over on 1 January 2027.
plain: No change to rates or service is announced. IDS said the delay to Access business mail price increases, due in October 2026, will affect Royal Mail's second-half financial performance.
why: The results show parcel volumes at Royal Mail and GLS up 8% each, with out-of-home networks of about 150,000 points a main growth driver.
tie: The results follow the 18 November 2026 announcement by GLS Group and Geopost of plans to combine their German parcel businesses.
syn: IDS reported first-half group revenue up 6.3% to £6.85 billion, with parcel volumes up 8% to 1.2 billion. Royal Mail revenue rose 3.9% to £4.13 billion with parcel volumes up 8% to 734 million, and GLS revenue rose 10.2% to £2.73 billion with volumes up 8% to 495 million. IDS said marketplace sellers and out-of-home options drove growth, and that the group now has around 150,000 out-of-home parcel points. It also said Royal Mail's second-half performance will be affected by the delay to Access business mail price increases that were due in October 2026.

aff.what: Royal Mail parcel volumes rose 8% to 734 million; its out-of-home network has 30,000 points, up from 13,000 three years ago.
Price increases due to take effect in October 2026 have been delayed, according to IDS.
GLS out-of-home volumes rose more than 50% year on year; its network grew 13% to around 117,000 locations.
GLS and Geopost (DPD in Germany) plan a combined business under the GLS brand with over €4 billion revenue.

title: Walmart U.S. eCommerce sales rise 23% as store-fulfilled delivery tops 40%
sum: Walmart reported 23% U.S. eCommerce sales growth for its fiscal 2027 third quarter in results released November 19, and raised its full-year outlook. According to its earnings presentation, U.S. store-fulfilled delivery grew more than 40%, and deliveries taking under three hours made up more than 37% of store-fulfilled orders.
plain: No change to rates or service for shippers. The item reports Walmart's own earnings and delivery volumes.
why: Walmart's store-fulfilled delivery grew over 40% in the quarter, a measure of how much of a major retailer's online volume ships from stores.
syn: Walmart reported 23% U.S. eCommerce sales growth for its fiscal 2027 third quarter on November 19, with global revenue of $188.8 billion, up 5.2%. Its earnings presentation showed U.S. store-fulfilled delivery growth above 40%, and deliveries taking under three hours were more than 37% of store-fulfilled orders. The MarketScale analysis notes that Reuters reported the quarter's online growth compared with 28% a year earlier, and that rising fuel and transportation costs complicated Walmart's price efforts.

title: UPS, FedEx raise Ground minimum charge to $12.70, analysis says
sum: UPS raises its Ground minimum charge 5.92% from $11.99 to $12.70 on Dec. 21, 2026, and FedEx raises its minimums on Jan. 4, 2027, according to an industry analysis. The analysis says a fixed-dollar minimum reduction loses value with each general rate increase (GRI), so net minimums rise faster than published ones.
plain: UPS minimum charges rise with the 2027 UPS Daily Rates on Dec. 21, 2026, and FedEx minimums rise on Jan. 4, 2027. Both carriers set the Ground minimum at $12.70, which can keep lightweight packages at or near list price.
why: An industry analysis says minimums affect up to 40% of its clients' packages, limiting the discount on lightweight parcels.

dates.w: UPS minimums rise with 2027 Daily Rates; Ground to $12.70
FedEx raises minimum charges; Ground to $12.70

sum: ConsumerAffairs reported on Nov. 19, 2026 that shipping gifts will cost more this holiday season because of higher base rates, transportation charges and seasonal surcharges. The article says consumers face higher delivery expenses and cites surveys showing strong resistance to paying shipping fees. The available text gives no carrier names or figures.

syn: ConsumerAffairs reported on Nov. 19, 2026 that shipping gifts will cost more this holiday season. title: Amazon confirms Prime Air drone delivery for Jacksonville; pad approved
sum: Amazon confirmed on November 19 that it is working to start Prime Air drone delivery in Jacksonville, Florida, in the coming months, according to DroneXL citing the Jax Daily Record. The city's Planning Commission approved a launch pad at 7489 Commonwealth Avenue the same day, including a cut in the required boundary setback from 500 feet to 29 feet.

syn: Amazon confirmed on November 19 that it is working with the FAA and local officials to start Prime Air drone delivery in Jacksonville, Florida, in the coming months, the Jax Daily Record reported. The same day, the city's Planning Commission approved an exception and a deviation for a launch pad at 7489 Commonwealth Avenue, cutting the required setback from 500 feet to 29 feet, the paper reported. DroneXL said the agenda does not name Amazon and that the results agenda was not yet posted on November 20, so any conditions are not public. Amazon told the paper Prime Air operates from 20 sites in 11 states, and DroneXL said Amazon's Prime Air site did not list Jacksonville on November 20.

title: DHL eCommerce survey: shipping options cause cart abandonment for one in three Black Friday shoppers
sum: DHL eCommerce's 2026 E-Commerce Trends Report, based on a survey of 29,000 online shoppers and 5,800 e-commerce businesses across 29 countries, was published in November 2026. It found that one in three Black Friday shoppers are most likely to abandon a purchase at the shipping-option stage, and that nearly nine in ten have used or plan to use AI to compare prices.

why: The survey covers 29,000 shoppers and 5,800 businesses and ties Black Friday purchase completion to delivery and returns options.
syn: DHL eCommerce's 2026 E-Commerce Trends Report surveyed 29,000 online shoppers and 5,800 e-commerce businesses across 29 countries. It found that one in three Black Friday shoppers are most likely to abandon a purchase at the shipping-option stage, and 77% would abandon a purchase if they did not trust the delivery or returns provider. Nine in ten prioritize fast, free delivery and easy returns, and more than half want same-day or faster services. The survey also found nearly nine in ten Black Friday shoppers have used AI to compare prices or plan to.

title: Former USPS inspector sentenced to over three years for stealing from parcels
sum: A former US Postal Service inspector, Scott Kelley, 52, was sentenced Wednesday in US District Court in Boston to more than three years in federal prison, the Boston Globe reported. He pleaded guilty in July to wire-fraud related charges. Prosecutors said he stole more than $340,000 in cash from nearly 2,000 flagged packages between 2019 and 2023.

sum: Industry experts told Supply Chain Dive that UPS shippers should plan for a possible Teamsters strike in 2028. The national contract covering about 300,000 UPS employees lasts through July 31, 2028. title: ITF Group report links part of $849.9B retail returns to carrier vetting
sum: ITF Group, a Missouri-based third-party logistics provider, says in its Retail Reality Check Report that many retail returns trace to how retailers vet and manage carriers. NRF projected consumers would return $849.9 billion in merchandise in 2025, equal to 15.8% of retail sales. ITF's report gives no figure for the share of returns tied to freight handling.

sum: Postmaster General David Steiner told the USPS Board of Governors on Nov. 10, 2026, that USPS will have fully developed plans in the first calendar quarter of 2027 to rationalize its retail footprint and non-First-Class Mail service standards. He said the agency faces a financial cliff within five years once the retiree health benefits fund is exhausted. Steiner also named Gary Reblin Chief Commercial Officer.
plain: No rates or service change take effect now. USPS said it will present plans in Q1 2027 that could change Marketing Mail service levels and the number of Post Offices.
why: USPS said package volume and revenue are growing, while possible service-standard changes for non-First-Class Mail remain under review for 2027.
tie: Steiner, who took over in July 2025, had told Congress that without new funding USPS may have to cut delivery days and close unprofitable post offices, as reported in September 2026.
new: Steiner spoke publicly at the Nov. 10, 2026, board meeting about USPS finances and named Gary Reblin Chief Commercial Officer; the remarks did not address the September report that he wanted to resign. For shippers, USPS said it will present plans for non-First-Class Mail service levels and Post Office numbers in Q1 2027.
syn: Postmaster General David Steiner told the USPS Board of Governors on Nov. 10, 2026, that the agency will have fully developed plans in the first calendar quarter of 2027 for changes to its retail and office footprint and to service standards for non-First-Class Mail. He said USPS faces a financial cliff within five years once the retiree health benefits fund is exhausted and that Congress must either remove or fund what he called uneconomical mandates. He said package volumes and revenue show single-digit volume growth and double-digit revenue growth in the first month of the new fiscal year.

aff.what: Steiner said USPS will need drastic changes to Marketing Mail service levels; plans are due in Q1 2027.
Steiner said USPS will need drastic changes in the number of Post Offices; plans are due in Q1 2027.
USPS said package volumes show single-digit growth and revenue double-digit growth in the first month of the new year.
Steiner said he expects service to improve from last year's strong improvement during peak season.

title: Amazon Prime Air wins first SAIL 4 approval from UK CAA
sum: Amazon said on 10 November 2026 that Prime Air is the first operator in the world to obtain a SAIL 4 Operating Authorisation and Flightworthiness Validation from the UK Civil Aviation Authority. The approval raises the number of eligible customers in Darlington from around 600 to roughly 8,000.
plain: Amazon's Prime Air drone deliveries in Darlington, UK, now reach roughly 8,000 eligible customers, up from around 600. No change to rates for other shippers.
why: The approval widens Amazon's UK drone delivery area in Darlington from around 600 to roughly 8,000 eligible customers.
syn: Amazon announced on 10 November 2026 that Prime Air has become the first operator in the world to obtain a SAIL 4 Operating Authorisation and Flightworthiness Validation from the UK Civil Aviation Authority. The CAA assessed Prime Air's operation, aircraft, organisation and approach to risk. Eligible customers in Darlington grow from around 600 to roughly 8,000, with deliveries in under two hours and approval to serve more densely populated communities in the area. Prime Air began operating in Darlington in early 2026 under authorisation for beyond-visual-line-of-sight flights in less densely populated areas.

aff.what: Eligible customers grow from around 600 to roughly 8,000, with delivery in under two hours.

aff.who: Prime Air operations in the UK
aff.what: Approval covers flights over more of Darlington, including more densely populated communities in the area.

title: USPS reports $6.5 billion net loss for fiscal 2026, down from $9.0 billion
sum: The U.S. Postal Service reported a GAAP net loss of $6.5 billion for the fiscal year ended Sept. 30, compared with $9.0 billion a year earlier. Operating revenue rose 3.0% to $82.9 billion. Shipping and Packages revenue rose 5.1% on a 5.3% volume decline, USPS said on Nov. 10, 2026.
plain: The results announcement sets no new rates or fees. USPS said price increases have been and will continue to be part of its strategy.
why: USPS's results show Shipping and Packages revenue up $1.7 billion as volume fell 359 million pieces, with USPS saying price increases will continue.
tie: USPS reported a $9.5 billion net loss for fiscal 2024 in November 2024, and a Postal Regulatory Commission analysis in May 2026 found fiscal 2025 competitive volume fell 6.0%.
new: USPS's fiscal 2026 results show Shipping and Packages revenue up 5.1% on 5.3% lower volume, and USPS said price increases will continue; the earlier coverage covered fiscal 2024 and 2025 results and a Nov. 4 congressional letter on borrowing.
syn: The U.S. Postal Service said on Nov. 10, 2026 that its net loss for fiscal 2026 was $6.5 billion, down $2.5 billion from $9.0 billion the prior year. Total operating revenue was $82.9 billion, up $2.4 billion, or 3.0%, and operating expenses were $89.4 billion, down $404 million. Shipping and Packages revenue rose $1.7 billion, or 5.1%, while volume fell 359 million pieces, or 5.3%. USPS attributed revenue growth to USPS Ground Advantage, price increases and a time-limited transportation-related increase for certain Shipping and Packages offerings. It also renewed its calls on Congress for reforms.

aff.what: Revenue rose $1.7 billion (5.1%) as volume fell 359 million pieces (5.3%) in fiscal 2026, USPS said.
USPS cited a transportation-related, time-limited price increase for certain offerings and said price increases will continue.
Net loss was $6.5 billion; controllable loss was $2.4 billion, against $2.7 billion the prior year.

title: Amazon wins UK CAA approval to expand Darlington drone delivery to 8,000
sum: The UK Civil Aviation Authority granted Amazon a SAIL 4 approval, which Amazon said allows Prime Air to expand drone deliveries in Darlington from 600 customers to around 8,000. Amazon said it is the first such approval in the world and opens the way to other UK towns and cities.
plain: Prime members in Darlington within 7.5 miles of the fulfilment centre can use drone delivery at no extra cost if items weigh 5 lbs or less. No change to rates for other shippers.
why: The approval lifts the Darlington Prime Air customer base from 600 to around 8,000 and is the basis for UK expansion, according to Amazon and the CAA.
tie: Amazon's August 2026 announcement of a Prime Air expansion to nearly 500 U.S. towns covered U.S. sites; this approval concerns the UK service in Darlington.
new: Amazon received UK CAA SAIL 4 approval to expand Darlington drone delivery from 600 to around 8,000 customers, extending the storyline beyond the U.S. to the UK, with no change to U.S. rules or fees.
syn: The UK Civil Aviation Authority has given Amazon a Specific Assurance and Integrity Level 4 (SAIL 4) approval for its Prime Air service, according to Motor Transport. Amazon said this lets it expand drone deliveries in Darlington from 600 customers to around 8,000, and that it is the first SAIL 4 approval in the world. The service launched in early 2026 using MK30 drones flying beyond visual line of sight in less densely populated areas. Amazon and the CAA said the approval opens the door to expansion in other UK towns and cities.

aff.what: Prime Air customer base expands from 600 to around 8,000, at no extra delivery cost.
Items of 5 lbs or less that fit a large shoebox, to gardens or driveways within 7.5 miles of the fulfilment centre.
Approval opens the way to expansion to other UK towns and cities, per Amazon and the CAA.

title: DHL eCommerce report finds 66% of US shoppers abandon carts over delivery options
sum: DHL eCommerce released U.S. findings from its 2026 eCommerce Trends Report ahead of the holiday season, on or before Nov. 10. It found 66% of U.S. shoppers abandon purchases when delivery offerings fall short, versus 48% of merchants who cite delivery as a reason. Fifty-seven percent of shoppers want same-day or faster delivery and returns within five years.
plain: No change to rates or service. The report describes survey findings on shopper and merchant attitudes toward delivery, inventory and AI.
why: The DHL eCommerce survey shows an 18-point gap between shoppers and merchants on delivery's role in cart abandonment, with same-day and next-day plans rising.

title: Amazon's Markham drone site hits 300-order daily cap; Homewood cites no warning
sum: Amazon's Markham, Illinois, drone delivery site has generally reached its maximum of 300 orders a day since flights began October 12, Amazon's Sam Bailey said at a November 10 ribbon-cutting, according to DroneXL. Homewood Mayor Rich Hofeld told the Chicago Tribune's Daily Southtown the village got no warning or communication from Amazon before the launch. Bailey said 21 MK30 drones fly from the site and that the Matteson warehouse launches next, without a date.
plain: Customers within 7.5 miles of the Markham site can receive drone deliveries, and Amazon told them to clear the yard and keep children indoors. Rates and fees are unchanged in this report.
why: Shows the Chicago-area Prime Air site running at its 300-order daily cap while local officials dispute notice, as Amazon scales drone delivery toward nearly 500 towns.
tie: The Markham launch follows Amazon's August 2026 plan to expand Prime Air to nearly 500 towns, including sites near Chicago, and DroneXL's March report that its Richardson, Texas, hub filled about 150 orders a day.
new: Amazon said Markham has generally hit its 300-order daily maximum with 21 drones and Homewood officials say they had no warning, while the FAA index still shows only the July draft; no change to shipper fees is reported.
syn: Amazon's Markham, Illinois, drone delivery site has generally hit its 300-order daily maximum since flights began October 12, Amazon economic development manager Sam Bailey said at a November 10 ribbon-cutting, according to DroneXL. Homewood Mayor Rich Hofeld told the Chicago Tribune's Daily Southtown that Amazon gave the village no warning before service started, while the FAA's July notice of the Chicago draft went to village officials, per the draft's Appendix A. Bailey said 21 MK30 drones fly from the site, 60% of the warehouse's inventory can go by drone, and Matteson launches next without a date. DroneXL reported that the FAA's environmental review index still lists only the July draft assessment for the Chicago sites, with no decision posted.

aff.what: Amazon says to clear the yard and keep children indoors during a delivery; the MK30 releases a package from about 12 feet.

aff.who: Homewood, Harvey, South Holland and Dolton residents
aff.what: Inside the 7.5-mile radius, per the Tribune; Homewood said it could not ground the drones.
Matteson warehouse launches next, Bailey said, without giving a date.

title: Scurri survey: 67% of UK shoppers would accept slower Peak delivery for lower cost
sum: Scurri research ahead of Peak 2026 found 67% of UK consumers would accept longer delivery times during Peak in return for free or cheaper delivery. Free delivery matters to 61%, against 29% who prioritise next day delivery and 13% same day. The findings come from two Scurri studies of UK retailers and consumers.
plain: No change to rates or service. The survey describes UK shopper preferences and retailer AI plans ahead of Peak 2026.
why: The survey indicates UK shoppers rank free delivery and delivery certainty above speed ahead of Peak 2026, with 61% prioritising free delivery.
syn: Scurri, a delivery management software provider, published findings from two studies of UK retailers and consumers carried out ahead of Peak 2026. Free delivery matters to 61% of consumers, compared with 29% prioritising next day delivery and 13% same day, and 67% would accept longer Peak delivery times for free or cheaper delivery. Among retailers, 58% say they are likely to use automated AI to manage ecommerce delivery strategy and carrier operations. Retailers estimate AI automation of carrier management could cut delivery costs by an average of 10.6%.

aff.what: 67% would accept longer delivery times in return for free or cheaper delivery; 47% would accept a late order if warned in advance.
58% are likely to use automated AI for delivery strategy and carrier operations; they estimate an average 10.6% delivery cost reduction.
53% say real-time tracking matters most and 44% prioritise an accurate delivery date.
88% say they should always be able to speak to a human and 85% want to know when they are dealing with AI.

title: Locus survey: 54% of shoppers abandoned a cart over delivery-date doubts
sum: Locus released its first Holiday Delivery Confidence Index on Nov. 10, based on a survey of 1,000 U.S. consumers. It found 54% abandoned an online cart in the past year because they were unsure an order would arrive when needed, and 37% paid extra for delivery by a specific date last holiday season.
plain: No change to rates or service. The survey reports that shoppers value a promised arrival date and that some pay extra for one.
why: The survey of 1,000 U.S. consumers links delivery-date certainty to online holiday purchase completion and to what shoppers pay for delivery.
syn: Locus, a last-mile dispatch software company, released its first annual Holiday Delivery Confidence Index on Nov. 10, surveying 1,000 U.S. consumers. According to the report, 54% abandoned an online shopping cart in the past year because they were unsure an order would arrive when needed, and 80% said a specific promised date would make them more likely to complete a holiday purchase. Lowest total cost was the top factor for 43% of shoppers and delivery-date certainty followed at 40%, while 8% ranked the fastest option first. A separate Radial survey found 70% of consumers would give up a 5% discount for guaranteed delivery on a specific date.

aff.what: 54% abandoned a cart in the past year over doubts about arrival timing; 71% of Gen Z and 27% of baby boomers did.
37% paid extra for delivery by a specific date last holiday season, including 52% of Gen Z and 9% of baby boomers.
80% said a promised date would make them more likely to complete a holiday purchase; 45% said much more likely.
69% consider three days or less appropriate; 52% expect holiday shipping to be as fast as or faster than usual.

title: Wing outlines Walmart drone delivery plan for Union Township
sum: Wing Aviation, owned by Alphabet, presented a plan to Union Township trustees on Tuesday to deliver Walmart orders by drone, possibly starting in January. Wing's permitting manager said the drones fly to single-family homes within six miles of the township Walmart and carry up to 2.5 pounds. The company is still seeking township permitting approval for its drone "nest."
plain: Walmart customers within six miles of the Union Township store could get drone delivery of packages up to 2.5 pounds as soon as January, free for Walmart Plus members. The start depends on township permitting approval.
why: Walmart Plus members within six miles of one store could get free drone delivery of packages up to 2.5 pounds, if the site is approved.
new: Wing, which was not in earlier coverage, is seeking approval for Walmart drone delivery in Union Township from as soon as January, alongside Walmart's Zipline expansion; it would be free for Walmart Plus members within six miles of the store.
syn: Wing Aviation, owned by Alphabet, told Union Township trustees on Tuesday that drones could begin delivering Walmart orders to residents as soon as January. A company representative said the drones fly autonomously at 55 miles per hour to single-family homes within six miles of the Walmart on Eastgate Square Drive, carrying packages up to 2.5 pounds. Wing still needs township permitting approval to build its "nest" near the store, and an administrator said the use would be approved under the zoning code. The company said it prefers to wait until three sites are permitted and complete before launching, and it is working on Walmart sites in Evendale and West Chester Township.

aff.what: Drone delivery would be free, within six miles of the Eastgate Square Drive store, as soon as January.

title: Nampa residents report Amazon Prime Air drone noise since Oct. 30 launch
sum: Residents near Amazon's Prime Air delivery zone in Nampa, Idaho, told Idaho News 6 that frequent drone flights are audible inside their homes and disrupt daily life. Amazon's Prime Air service began in Nampa on October 30, and one resident said she has looked at homes elsewhere.
plain: No change to rates or service for shippers. The report concerns neighbor complaints about Prime Air drone noise in Nampa.
why: Resident complaints in Nampa show community reaction to Prime Air as Amazon plans drone delivery in almost 500 towns.
tie: Amazon said in August 2026 that Prime Air would reach almost 500 cities and towns by the end of 2026.
new: Residents in Nampa, where Prime Air began Oct. 30, are voicing noise complaints, the first local reaction in this storyline; the report states no change to shipper prices or service.
syn: Neighbors living near Amazon's Prime Air delivery zone in Nampa, Idaho, said the drone flights are constant and can be heard indoors with windows and doors closed, according to Idaho News 6. Amazon's Prime Air service started in Nampa on October 30. One resident said she has looked at homes elsewhere, and the city's information page says residents can contact Amazon or file a complaint with the FAA.

aff.what: Residents said drone buzzing is audible indoors and outdoors; the service began Oct. 30.

title: ShipBob opens Bobby AI agent to all brands on its platform
sum: ShipBob said on Nov. 10 that Bobby, its in-dashboard AI agent, is available to every brand on its fulfillment platform. Bobby answers fulfillment questions and acts on them, and shows each change and waits for approval before it runs. Per Tech Times, the same edits can be made from Claude or ChatGPT through ShipBob's MCP connector, where the AI app sets the approval prompts.
plain: Every ShipBob brand can use Bobby in the dashboard to query and change fulfillment operations, with changes waiting for the brand's approval. No change to ShipBob rates or fees was announced.
why: ShipBob says its teams fulfill more than 100 million orders annually, and every brand on the platform can now use the agent to change live orders.
tie: Tech Times reported that ShipBob described Bobby as a beta with a waitlist in August 2026 and planned general availability for fall.
syn: ShipBob said Bobby, its in-dashboard AI agent, is now available to every brand on its platform. Bobby answers fulfillment questions in plain language and can act on them, such as rerouting shipments or clearing stuck orders, and waits for approval before changing anything. According to Tech Times, the same edits can be made through ShipBob's MCP connector from AI apps such as Claude and ChatGPT, where ShipBob's documentation says the AI app controls approval prompts, not ShipBob. ShipBob said its teams fulfill more than 100 million orders annually.

aff.what: Bobby is available to every brand in the dashboard; read access is on by default and account owners decide who can make changes.
Bobby can reroute shipments, substitute out-of-stock items in bulk, create replacement orders and flag 30-day stockout risk.
Edits through the MCP connector rely on the AI app's approval prompts; ShipBob's server does not enforce one, per Tech Times.

title: Amazon opens Prime Air drone delivery center in Markham, Ill.
sum: Amazon cut the ribbon on a Prime Air drone delivery center at its IGQ1 fulfillment center in Markham, Illinois, on Tuesday, the Chicago-area debut of the service, the Chicago Sun-Times reported. Deliveries are set to begin "this fall" from the site at 2201 W. 159th St., according to the company. The drones carry packages weighing up to five pounds.
plain: Amazon's Prime Air drone delivery is due to start from the Markham site this fall, for packages up to five pounds. The sources give no change to rates for other shippers.
why: Amazon's drone network is moving from announcement to a first Chicago-area site, with a five-pound package limit that bounds what the service can carry.
tie: The opening follows Amazon's August 2026 announcement that it was expanding drone delivery to suburban areas in nearly 500 U.S. cities, including the Chicago metro area.
new: Amazon's August plan for Chicago-area drone deliveries now has a physical site in Markham, with deliveries set to begin "this fall" for packages up to five pounds.
syn: Amazon held a ribbon-cutting on Tuesday for a Prime Air drone delivery center at its IGQ1 fulfillment center in Markham, Illinois, the Chicago-area debut of the service. According to the company, drone deliveries are set to begin "this fall" from the site. Amazon says the drones can deliver everyday items in as fast as 30 minutes and can carry only packages weighing up to five pounds. The Sun-Times noted challenges including noise concerns, tree cover and pools that can make drop-off zones hard to find.

aff.what: Drone deliveries are set to begin "this fall" from the Markham center, with items delivered in as fast as 30 minutes.
The drones can carry only packages weighing up to five pounds.
Drones will primarily fly in suburbs, with each drone site serving multiple cities.

title: Wing starts Walmart drone delivery in Memphis area, free in apps
sum: Wing began delivering Walmart orders by drone on Nov. 10 from three Supercenters in Bartlett and Cordova, Tennessee, and West Memphis, Arkansas, according to DroneXL. A Wing spokesperson said delivery is free in the Wing and Walmart apps. Each flight carries up to 2.75 pounds.
plain: Shoppers near three Memphis-area Walmart stores can order by drone through the Walmart app, Walmart.com or Wing's app. Wing says delivery is free in the Wing and Walmart apps, and each flight carries up to 2.75 pounds.
why: Memphis is Wing's sixth U.S. metro with Walmart and the first of seven cities named in June; Amazon's Memphis service is still listed as coming soon.
tie: Wing and Walmart named Memphis in June among seven cities, and Wing said at its July Orlando launch that the payload limit would rise to five pounds.
new: Memphis became the first of the seven cities named in June to start Walmart drone deliveries, with Wing saying delivery is free in its apps and a 2.75-pound limit per flight.
syn: Wing began delivering Walmart orders by drone in the Memphis area on Nov. 10, from Supercenters in Bartlett and Cordova, Tennessee, and West Memphis, Arkansas, according to DroneXL. It is Wing's first Tennessee market and its sixth U.S. metro with Walmart, and the first of seven cities named in June to start service. A Wing spokesperson told DroneXL on Nov. 12 that delivery is free in the Wing and Walmart apps. Amazon quoted Memphis prices at a June event, and its Prime Air site still lists the city as "Coming soon", DroneXL reported.

title: ShipStation Global runs more than 250 AI agents across freight operations
sum: ShipStation Global said it has deployed more than 250 purpose-built AI agents in production, including one that takes an emailed quote request through carrier selection and booking without a dispatcher. Executives described the system in an FreightWaves interview. The company said it serves more than one million annual customers.
plain: No change to rates or service is announced. ShipStation Global says its AI agents speed up quoting and booking for its freight customers.
why: The company says it serves more than one million annual customers, with a focus on SMB shippers that lack staff and budget to build such automation.
syn: ShipStation Global, formed from the combination of legacy WEX Group and Octane, said it has more than 250 AI agents in production across its freight operations. One agent handles an emailed quote request through carrier selection and booking without a human dispatcher, which the company said resolved a Sunday evening inquiry from a China-based shipper within minutes. Executives Joel Clum and the company's CTO described the system in an interview with FreightWaves. The company is aiming the tools at small and mid-sized shippers and said it has more than one million annual customers.

aff.what: ShipStation says the AI tools give them automation for quoting, booking and carrier selection that they often lack staff to build.
One agent books from an emailed quote request in minutes, ShipStation said, instead of waiting for a dispatcher.
Clum said carrier vetting has increased dramatically, with escorts and checkpoint verification for certain loads.
Clum said they are deepening existing broker and carrier relationships, citing liability and cargo theft risk.

title: USPS first-class on-time rate reaches 89.03% for fiscal 2026
sum: USPS delivered 89.03% of first-class mail on time in fiscal 2026, up from 83.15% in 2025, Greg White told the USPS Board of Governors. Postmaster General David Steiner said the agency may close post offices and change service standards for non-first-class and marketing mail if Congress does not act, with plans due in the first quarter of calendar 2027.
plain: No rate change was announced. USPS said it may change service standards for non-first-class and marketing mail, with plans due in the first quarter of calendar 2027.
why: USPS said service standards for non-first-class and marketing mail could change if Congress does not act, which would reach shippers of those mail classes.
tie: The meeting followed USPS's Nov. 10, 2026 report of a $6.5 billion fiscal 2026 net loss and a Nov. 4, 2026 postal caucus letter on the agency's borrowing authority.
new: The Board of Governors meeting added fiscal 2026 on-time figures (89.03% for first-class mail), a $85.8 billion fiscal 2027 revenue goal and Steiner's statement that closure and service-standard plans will come in the first quarter of 2027, which could affect non-first-class and marketing mail shippers.
syn: USPS delivered 89.03% of first-class mail on time in fiscal 2026, compared with 83.15% in 2025, and met its 89% composite target for the first time since 2022, USPS executive Greg White told the Board of Governors. Postmaster General David Steiner said USPS will need to close post offices and change service standards for non-first-class and marketing mail if Congress does not act. He said he will have plans in the first quarter of calendar 2027. Chief Financial Officer Luke Grossman set a fiscal 2027 revenue goal of $85.8 billion.

aff.what: On-time delivery was 89.03% in fiscal 2026 versus 83.15% in 2025; the average delivery time was 0.4 days faster.
Steiner said service standards could change if Congress does not act; plans are due in the first quarter of calendar 2027.
Steiner said post office closures are possible if Congress does not act.

title: FedEx adds duty and tax payment to its FedEx Import Tool
sum: FedEx added an integrated duty and tax payment function to its FedEx Import Tool (FiT), The Manila Times reported. Customers can handle document submission, clearance processing, tracking and payment on one digital platform, FedEx said. The tool is available in the Philippines and several other Asia-Pacific markets.
plain: Importers using FiT in the Philippines can now pay duties and taxes online with cards, e-wallets or bank transfers. FedEx said FiT is free for account holders and customers without accounts.
why: FiT is free to account holders and non-account consignees in the Philippines and eight other Asia-Pacific markets, putting import payment on one platform.
syn: FedEx has added an integrated duty and tax payment function to the FedEx Import Tool (FiT), according to The Manila Times. Customers can pay by card, e-wallet or bank transfer. FiT is free and is available in the Philippines, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand.

title: OTAA fulfills US orders from Texas via Cart.com as de minimis ends
sum: Australia-based OTAA, which makes ties and cufflinks, is fulfilling U.S. orders from a facility in Longview, Texas, through a partnership with Cart.com, Supply Chain Dive reported on Nov. 10, 2026. The report links the move to the end of de minimis.

title: Dollar General adds Instacart same-day delivery at about 20,000 stores
sum: Dollar General and its subsidiary pOpshelf have introduced same-day delivery through the Instacart Marketplace, according to Retail Insight Network. The service covers around 20,000 stores across 48 US states.
plain: Shoppers can order same-day delivery from about 20,000 Dollar General and pOpshelf stores through Instacart. No change to carrier rates or surcharges is reported.
why: Same-day delivery now reaches about 20,000 Dollar General and pOpshelf stores in 48 states through a third-party marketplace.
syn: Dollar General and its subsidiary pOpshelf have introduced same-day delivery through the Instacart Marketplace, Retail Insight Network reported on 2026-11-11. aff.what: Same-day delivery via the Instacart Marketplace at around 20,000 stores in 48 US states.

title: California privacy agency fines FedEx $2.975M over ad-tracking opt-outs
sum: The California Privacy Protection Agency fined FedEx $2.975 million over alleged violations of the state's privacy law, MediaPost reported on Nov. 10, 2026. The agency said FedEx misrepresented its online behavioral advertising practices and did not honor opt-out signals such as the Global Privacy Control. FedEx agreed to the order without admitting or denying the findings.
plain: No change to rates or service. The agency said the personal information involved did not include shipping data.
why: The order concerns FedEx's website advertising data practices, not shipping data, and sets a fine of $2.975 million under California's privacy law.
syn: The California Privacy Protection Agency fined FedEx $2.975 million over alleged violations of the California Consumer Privacy Act, according to MediaPost. The agency said FedEx shared website visitors' personal information with ad-tech companies between July 1, 2023 and October 27, 2025, and did not properly honor opt-out signals such as the Global Privacy Control. FedEx agreed to the order without admitting or denying the findings. The agency said the data did not include shipping data, and MLex reported that FedEx also agreed to adjust its business practices.

sum: Westborough's Planning Board accepted Amazon's request on November 10 to withdraw its site-plan application for a Prime Air drone hub at 64 Otis Street, without prejudice, according to DroneXL. title: Amazon launches Prime Air drone delivery from Markham, Illinois
sum: Amazon held a ribbon-cutting on Tuesday for its Prime Air drone delivery service at its Markham, Ill., fulfillment center, which Amazon said has operated since Oct. 12. title: GOFO white paper says US last-mile market is realigning
sum: GOFO, a last-mile delivery carrier, highlighted a white paper titled How Fragmenting E-Commerce Is Rebuilding the U.S. Last Mile in a Nov. 9, 2026 release. Citing ShipMatrix data, it said US domestic parcel volume reached 23.9 billion packages in 2025, up 0.4%, with Amazon Logistics ahead of USPS at 6.7 billion packages versus 6.6 billion.

title: NYC Councilman Wong pulls co-sponsorship of Delivery Protection Act
sum: Queens Councilman Phil Wong removed his name as co-sponsor of the Delivery Protection Act, citing job losses at small businesses, the New York Post reported. The bill would require Amazon to license its 15 last-mile facilities in the city and hire delivery workers directly. Speaker Julie Menin has not taken a stance, and the Law Department is reviewing the bill.
plain: No rates or service have changed. If the bill passes, Amazon-commissioned research estimates New Yorkers' delivery costs would rise by $664 a year, or about $5.20 per package.
why: The bill would be the first of its kind in a US city and would affect over 5,000 delivery workers at about 40 contractors, per Amazon.

The bill, introduced by Councilmember Tiffany Cabán, would require Amazon to get licenses for its 15 last-mile facilities in the city and hire delivery workers as full-timers, and it would also apply to other companies including FedEx. Speaker Julie Menin has voiced concern about job losses and higher prices, and the Law Department is reviewing the bill, including whether federal law preempts it, according to sources cited by the Post.

title: NRF: September imports hit 2.37M TEU, busiest month of 2026
sum: The National Retail Federation and Hackett Associates said in the Global Port Tracker report released Nov. 9 that U.S. ports handled 2.37 million TEU of loaded imports in September, up 12.6% year over year. The report projects imports to taper through year-end, with 2026 totaling 26 million TEU, up 2% from 25.4 million TEU last year.

The tracker projects October at 2.26 million TEU, November at 2.05 million TEU and December at 2.03 million TEU, bringing 2026 to 26 million TEU, up 2% from 25.4 million TEU in 2025. title: USPS asks PRC to change data source in Priority Mail cost model
sum: The Postal Service petitioned the Postal Regulatory Commission on Nov. 6, 2026, to replace ODIS-RPW sample data with Product Tracking and Reporting (PTR) data in its Priority Mail transportation model. The Commission opened Docket No. RM2027-3, with comments due Nov. 27, 2026.

title: UPS sues CBP at trade court to recover IEEPA tariff refunds
sum: UPS and two affiliates sued U.S. Customs and Border Protection at the U.S. Court of International Trade, The Loadstar reported. They want CBP ordered to re-liquidate entries and refund IEEPA duties plus interest. UPS has received about $500 million from CBP and had passed about $230 million to customers by Sept. 30, according to its third-quarter filing.

They seek an order for CBP to re-liquidate entries, including finally liquidated ones, and refund IEEPA duties with interest. The Supreme Court ruled on Feb. 20 that the law did not let the president impose the tariffs, according to Supply Chain 24/7. CBP says it needs a court order before repaying finally liquidated entries. UPS says customers paid the duties in many cases and that it would pass recovered funds to them.

title: FedEx adds 567,000 kg weekly Asia Pacific-U.S. air capacity
sum: FedEx said on November 3, 2026 that it has added 567,000 kilograms (1.25 million pounds) of weekly capacity between Asia Pacific and the United States. The new five-times-weekly Boeing 777F service routes via Anchorage to the Memphis World Hub, with a separate five-times-weekly connection to Dallas-Fort Worth.

Homewood told its residents on Oct. 26 that it cannot ground or quiet the drones, per the Country Herald. It also reported that 15 states have asked the Second Circuit to set aside the FAA's July 28 national environmental finding. title: Parcel market shifts as private networks and new carriers grow, DC Velocity reports
sum: DC Velocity reported views from Ryder, Gartner, Davinci Micro Fulfillment and OnTrac on a parcel market with more carrier choices and more complex pricing. Gartner's Chris Kina said the market is softening while carriers add surcharges. OnTrac's Vijay Ramachandram said UPS and FedEx combined have changed rates more than 20 times in 18 months.
plain: No change to rates or service. The article gives industry views on pricing complexity, new carriers and retailer-run delivery networks.
why: Shippers face more carrier choices and more frequent UPS and FedEx rate changes, according to executives quoted in the feature.
syn: DC Velocity collected industry views on a parcel market it describes as changing rapidly. Gartner's Chris Kina said the market is softening rather than expanding, and that carriers keep adding surcharges despite weak or declining volumes, which he called a margin-defense move. He said asset-light providers using AI promise up to 40% price savings, and that Walmart has expanded store fulfillment delivery to cover 93% of the population. OnTrac's Vijay Ramachandram said UPS and FedEx combined have changed rates more than 20 times in the last 18 months, which makes price certainty harder for shippers using several carriers.

aff.what: Ramachandram said frequent rate changes make price certainty harder as spend is spread across more carriers.
Kina said their footprint and asset advantage is being chipped away by local, regional and specialist providers.
Kina said retailers are investing billions in private networks that he expects to gain parcel market share.
Ramachandram said retailers are raising free-shipping minimums, so order and package sizes are rising.

title: Scurri survey: 67% of shoppers would accept slower Peak delivery for lower cost
sum: Scurri research of UK retailers and consumers found 67% of shoppers would accept longer delivery times during Peak in return for free or cheaper delivery. Free delivery matters to 61%, against 29% for next day and 13% for same day. Retailers are accelerating AI use, with 58% likely to use automated AI to manage delivery strategy and carrier operations.
plain: No change to rates or service. The research reports UK shopper and retailer attitudes ahead of Peak 2026.
why: The Scurri studies of UK retailers and consumers point to price and delivery certainty over speed ahead of Peak 2026.
syn: Scurri published two studies of UK retailers and consumers ahead of Peak 2026. They found 67% of shoppers would accept longer delivery times during Peak in return for free or cheaper delivery, and 61% say free delivery matters, compared with 29% for next day and 13% for same day. Retailers are turning to AI for efficiency, with 58% likely to use automated AI to manage delivery strategy and carrier operations, and they estimate AI automation of carrier management could cut delivery costs by an average of 10.6%. Scurri's CEO Rory O'Connor said Peak will be a reality check for retail AI.

aff.what: 53% say real-time tracking matters most, 44% an accurate delivery date; 47% would accept a late Peak order if warned.
58% likely to use automated AI for delivery strategy and carrier operations; estimated average cost cut of 10.6%.
88% want the option to speak to a human and 85% want to know when they are dealing with AI.

title: Walmart and Wing open drone delivery ceremony in West Memphis
sum: Walmart, Wing and West Memphis, Arkansas officials held a ribbon-cutting Monday for what the city called the Mid-South's first drone delivery service. WREG reported the service was not yet available in West Memphis at about 3 p.m. that day. Standard delivery fees apply per order, and Walmart+ members can get free drone delivery on eligible orders for a limited time, the city said.
